messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 37-year-old psychologist who came to therapy six months after he was raped by a male colleague during a professional conference. The assault occurred in the colleague’s hotel room, a space Kofi had entered willingly, believing they were meeting to discuss a collaborative research project. The door clicked shut automatically behind him, and within moments, the conversation shifted into something he could not have predicted and could not stop. He froze, his body going still as his mind scrambled to make sense of what was happening. Afterwards, he dressed in silence, walked out of the room, and flew home the next morning without telling anyone.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi found himself unable to sit in his own office at the community mental health center where he worked. The room had a door that locked from the inside, and every time he closed it to begin a session, he felt his chest tighten and his breathing grow shallow. He began leaving the door slightly ajar, then propping it open with a chair, then eventually asking a colleague if he could use a shared space instead. He told himself it was about ventilation, about needing more light. But he knew the truth: being in a locked or confined room made him feel like he was back in that hotel, and he had come to believe that he could not stop bad things from happening to him, that his body and his will were not his own. This sense of helplessness became the lens through which he saw everything. He felt that others could see what had happened to him just by looking at him, as though the assault was written on his skin. He started avoiding eye contact with male clients, especially those who reminded him of the colleague, and he began scheduling his sessions so that he was never alone in the building with another man. What frightened him most was the certainty that he had no future—that the life he had been building, the career he had worked for, was already over.

These negative appraisals fed directly into a state of constant threat. Kofi could not relax, even in places he logically knew were safe. At home, he slept on the couch with his back against the armrest, facing the door, because he felt unsafe unless his back was against a wall where he could see the room. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, his ears tuned to every creak and footstep. The vigilance was exhausting, but he could not let it go. He was certain that if he let his guard down, something else would happen. And this vigilance, in turn, reinforced his belief that he was fundamentally exposed and helpless. The more he scanned for danger, the more dangerous the world felt. He began to withdraw from social life entirely, declining invitations from friends and canceling plans at the last minute. His supervisor noticed that he seemed distracted and asked if everything was all right. Kofi said he was tired, and left it at that.

The threat also intensified his sensitivity to triggers. One afternoon, a female colleague mentioned a news article about sexual violence in the workplace, and Kofi felt his stomach drop. He excused himself to the restroom and stood with his hands on the sink, breathing slowly, trying to push the memory back down. Comments on sexual trauma cues had become unbearable. They pulled him into the moment of the assault with a vividness that felt like reliving it. He also found himself increasingly uncomfortable being alone with men, even those he had known for years. He started timing his arrivals and departures to avoid walking through the corridor at the same time as male coworkers. He knew this was changing how he worked, how he lived, but he could not see a way out. He had begun to believe that the assault had not only happened to him but had also revealed something true about the world—that safety was an illusion, and that he would never feel it again.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a session with a new client, a man who spoke in a soft, measured tone that reminded him of the colleague. Kofi felt his hands go cold, his mind go blank, and for a full thirty seconds he could not speak. He ended the session early and sat in his car in the parking lot, shaking. He realized he could not keep doing this—could not keep pretending that the door was open for ventilation, could not keep arranging his life around a terror he refused to name. He was most afraid that therapy would not work, that the hopelessness was correct, that his future really was gone. But he was also afraid of what it might mean if he started to feel safe again—whether that would mean forgiving, or forgetting, or betraying what had happened. He came to the first session wanting to know if it was possible to live without the wall at his back, and not knowing if he was ready to find out.
